hints.S11_A1: An ARROW is shot from a bow, and the train was THERE AND GONE IN SECONDS. Ask: is the missing word about weight, about noise, or about speed? In 'as ___ as', the adjective must match what the arrow is famous for.
hints.S11_A2: You have just got INTO THE CAR and Father is talking about SEATBELTS. Ask: does he want them taken off, broken or lost - or clicked firmly into place? A safety instruction always tells you to secure something, never to undo it.
hints.S11_A3: They are TIRED and want to REACH THEIR HOTEL, so they must leave the TAXI behind. Ask: which phrasal verb means to climb down from a vehicle? 'Break into' means to force your way in, and 'stay in' would keep them inside.
hints.S11_A4: Anya COUNTED DOWN THE HOURS and her plane has finally LANDED. Ask: does this idiom describe illness, trouble, confusion - or pure delight? An idiom cannot be read word by word; learn it as one whole phrase.
hints.S11_A5: The BRANCH lies on the road, yet the cyclist CONTINUED RIDING SAFELY - so he went round it without touching it. Ask: which verb means to turn sharply aside to avoid something? 'Crashed' hits it and 'stopped' would end the ride.
hints.S11_B1: The subject is NOBODY, not the crowd on the PLATFORM. Words like nobody and everyone act like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the verb ending in -s?
hints.S11_B2: HAS is already sitting in the sentence, so the blank must partner with it. Ask: after 'has', do we use the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle? Only one of them builds a present perfect.
hints.S11_B3: The bus PULLED UP suddenly, cutting across something that was already going on in the QUEUE. Ask: which form shows an action still in progress in the past? A plain past verb only reports a finished action.
hints.S11_B4: THAN tells you two roads are being compared, and 'fast' is a short adjective. Ask: do short adjectives add -er, or do they need 'most' in front? Never glue 'more' onto a word that already carries the -er ending.
hints.S11_B5: EVERY PASSENGER means each one on their own, so the subject counts as ONE. Ask: does a singular subject take a singular verb or a plural one? The rule applies right now, in the present, so a past form cannot be right.
hints.S11_B6: The statement already runs on CAN ('can be extremely crowded'), and it is positive. Ask: after a positive statement, does the tag turn negative or stay positive? The tag must reuse the SAME helping verb.
hints.S11_B7: The blank sits right before the noun BAGS, so it must show who owns them. Ask: can a subject pronoun ever describe a noun? A possessive form is needed - but not the standalone kind that ends a sentence.
hints.S11_B8: The other verb in the sentence is WAVED - a finished past action. Ask: should both verbs in one story share the same tense? This verb is regular, so what ending must it take, and what happens to its final letter?
hints.S11_C1: The verb LOVES stands right in front of the blank. Ask: after love, like or enjoy, does the next verb take 'to' or the -ing ending? LOVE + verb-ing is a fixed pattern that never changes.
hints.S11_C2: The subject is HE, and he ALWAYS follows the traffic rules - a habit that is true every day. Ask: in the simple present, what does a singular subject add to the plain verb?
hints.S11_C3: LAST YEAR fixes this firmly in finished past time. Ask: is this verb regular or irregular? Adding -ed to it is the classic mistake - the vowel inside the word changes instead.
hints.S11_C4: WHILE signals a longer action already running when the WATERFALL appeared, and the subject counts as ONE person. Ask: which past form shows an action still going on - a finished simple past, or a helper plus the -ing form?
hints.S11_C5: The subject THE OTHER CARS names more than one thing, and they all moved slowly at that same past moment. Ask: which helper does a plural subject need in the past continuous - the singular one, or the plural one?
hints.S11_C6: The verb just before the blank is WANTS. Ask: after want, hope or decide, does English use the -ing form, or the infinitive? WANT + infinitive never varies - and an infinitive always carries its own little marker word in front.
hints.S11_C7: SHOULD is a modal verb, and a modal is always followed by the bare verb. Ask: can you ever add -s or -ing after should, must or can? Keep the verb in its plainest form.
hints.S11_C8: RIGHT NOW - she sits behind the wheel at this very moment, on her FIRST LESSON. Ask: which form shows an action happening as we speak, and which helper goes with a singular subject - the singular one, or the plural one?
hints.S11_D1: The family reach the AIRPORT TWO HOURS BEFORE this moment, so the plane has not left yet. Ask: does the box word name the leaving or the arriving? 'Arrival' belongs to the other end of the journey.
hints.S11_D2: The plane still flies - it simply leaves ANOTHER THREE HOURS later because of the THUNDERSTORM. Ask: is the flight scrapped altogether, or only pushed back? 'Cancelled' would mean it never leaves at all.
hints.S11_D3: The announcement finally calls them to WALK ONTO THE PLANE. Ask: which box word names the act of getting on board a plane or ship? It is not the moment of leaving - that word is used in blank 1.
hints.S11_D4: They are already IN THE AIR when something makes the plane SHAKE so badly that seatbelts must be fastened. Ask: does the box word name a landing, a delay, or rough and bumpy air? Match it to the shaking.
hints.S11_D5: At the end they step out into THE BUSY STREETS OF TOKYO. Ask: does the blank name the ACT of arriving, or the PLACE they were travelling to all along? 'Arrival' names the act, not the place.
hints.S11_E1: The underlined word means 'at this place', but the sentence is about the SOUND of rain reaching your ears. Ask: which spelling belongs to your ears? The two sound identical, so choose by meaning, not by sound.
hints.S11_E2: TAKE is an irregular verb, so the -ed rule can never apply to it. Ask: how would you say it in the past - 'yesterday the driver ___ a rest'? Irregular verbs change shape instead of adding an ending.
hints.S11_E3: The underlined word is describing MOVED - an action, not a thing. Ask: do we describe HOW an action happens with an adjective, or with an adverb? A road can be smooth; the way a bus travels needs the -ly form.
hints.S11_E4: Every other verb in this story is past: MOVED, FELL, ARRIVED. Ask: is the underlined verb in the same tense as the rest? It is a regular verb - what ending does it need, and what happens to its final -t?
hints.S11_E5: The REPORT belongs to the drivers - more than one person. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or does it only make a plural? Work out where the apostrophe must go when the owners are many.
hints.S11_F1: The CONDUCTOR is reporting a yes/no question. Ask three things: which little linking word must follow ASKED? Does the reported question keep question word order, or normal statement order? And what happens to 'you' and 'your'?
hints.S11_F2: One action was already going on; the other happened all at once. Ask: which of the two is the long background action, and which one cuts in? WHEN goes in front of the sudden event - and never drop the helping verb.
